recipe: Merge two or more state variables into a single state variable when they always change together, so you don't forget to keep them in sync.
trigger_condition: You have two or more state variables that are always updated at the same time in the same event handler.
evidence: if some two state variables always change together, it might be a good idea to unify them into a single state variable.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Remove a state variable and instead calculate its value during rendering from props or other existing state variables.
trigger_condition: A state variable's value can always be derived from the component's props or other state variables.
evidence: If you can calculate some information from the component's props or its existing state variables during rendering, you should not put that information into that component's state.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Structure state in a flat way rather than deeply hierarchical when possible, to make updates more convenient.
trigger_condition: Your state is organized in a deeply nested object structure that is inconvenient to update.
evidence: Deeply hierarchical state is not very convenient to update. When possible, prefer to structure state in a flat way.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Reduce duplication when the same data exists across multiple state variables or within nested objects, to make it easier to keep them in sync.
trigger_condition: The same data is stored in more than one state variable or in multiple places within nested state objects.
evidence: When the same data is duplicated between multiple state variables, or within nested objects, it is difficult to keep them in sync. Reduce duplication when you can.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: When tracking a selected item from a list, store only its ID in state and derive the full object during render by looking it up in the list.
trigger_condition: You have a list of objects in state and a separate state variable holding one of those objects, creating duplicated data.
evidence: Instead of a `selectedItem` object (which creates a duplication with objects inside `items`), you hold the `selectedId` in state, and *then* get the `selectedItem` by searching the `items` array for an item with that ID
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Only keep the essential state in your state variables; compute derived values during render instead of storing them separately.
trigger_condition: You find yourself maintaining two state variables that represent the same underlying data, causing them to fall out of sync.
evidence: you didn't need to hold *the selected item* in state, because only the *selected ID* is essential. The rest could be calculated during render.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Structure your state as a flat (normalized) object keyed by ID rather than deeply nested, so that updating nested items requires fewer levels of state changes and avoids data duplication across branches.
trigger_condition: You are managing a tree-like or hierarchical data structure in React state and find updates cumbersome or error-prone.
evidence: You can nest state as much as you like, but making it "flat" can solve numerous problems. It makes state easier to update, and it helps ensure you don't have duplication in different parts of a nested object.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: When removing an item from a normalized state, update only two levels: filter the child ID out of the parent's childIds array, then replace the parent entry in the root object with the updated version.
trigger_condition: You need to delete a node from a normalized (flat) state structure in React.
evidence: In order to remove a place now, you only need to update two levels of state:

recipe: Create the updated parent object by spreading the existing parent and replacing its childIds with a filtered array that excludes the removed child ID.
trigger_condition: You are removing a child from a parent's childIds in a normalized React state.
evidence:
childIds: parent.childIds
        .filter(id => id !== childId)

recipe: Update the root state object by spreading the existing plan and using a computed key to replace only the parent entry with its updated version.
trigger_condition: You need to write the new root state after modifying a single parent in a normalized React state.

recipe: To improve memory usage, recursively remove the deleted item and all its descendants from the table object, not just from the parent's childIds.
trigger_condition: You are removing items from a normalized state and want to free memory rather than just hiding the item from the parent.
evidence: Ideally, you would also remove the deleted items (and their children!) from the "table" object to improve memory usage.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: If two state variables always update together, merge them into a single state variable.
trigger_condition: You notice two separate state variables that are always set or changed in the same event handler.
evidence: If two state variables always update together, consider merging them into one.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Choose your state variables carefully to avoid creating impossible states.
trigger_condition: You are designing or refactoring the state shape of a component and want to ensure every combination of state values is valid.
evidence: Choose your state variables carefully to avoid creating "impossible" states.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Structure your state in a way that reduces the chances you will make a mistake updating it.
trigger_condition: You are organizing complex state and want to make incorrect updates harder to write.
evidence: Structure your state in a way that reduces the chances that you'll make a mistake updating it.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Avoid redundant and duplicate state so that you don't need to keep it in sync.
trigger_condition: You have derived values stored as separate state that could be computed from existing state.
evidence: Avoid redundant and duplicate state so that you don't need to keep it in sync.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Don't put props into state unless you specifically want to prevent updates.
trigger_condition: A child component receives a prop that changes over time and you are tempted to copy it into local state.
evidence: Don't put props *into* state unless you specifically want to prevent updates.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: For UI patterns like selection, keep an ID or index in state instead of the object itself.
trigger_condition: You are implementing a selection or highlight feature and considering whether to store the selected object or just its identifier.
evidence: For UI patterns like selection, keep ID or index in state instead of the object itself.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: If updating deeply nested state is complicated, try flattening it.
trigger_condition: Your state is deeply nested and updating a value requires multiple levels of spread or map operations.
evidence: If updating deeply nested state is complicated, try flattening it.
source_name: react.dev learn: Choosing the State Structure

recipe: Reduce state nesting by moving ephemeral UI state into child components when it doesn't need to be stored.
trigger_condition: You have transient UI state such as hover or focus that only matters within a single component.
evidence: Sometimes, you can also reduce state nesting by moving some of the nested state into the child components. This works well for ephemeral UI state that doesn't need to be stored, like whether an item is hovered.

recipe: Remove redundant state variables that can be derived from existing state. Calculate derived values (like counts) during render from the source-of-truth array instead of storing them as separate state.
trigger_condition: You have state variables that duplicate information already derivable from another state variable, causing them to go out of sync.
evidence: They are redundant because you can always calculate the number of items (packed or total) from the `items` array itself. Remove the redundant state to fix the bug:

recipe: When an object exists in an array in state, store only its identifier in separate state rather than the object itself, so comparisons remain valid after the array is updated.
trigger_condition: You store an object in one state variable and the same object (or its data) in an array in another state variable, and you need to compare them for rendering.
evidence: Instead of storing *the letter itself* in two places, store the `highlightedId` instead. Then you can check `isHighlighted` for each letter with `letter.id === highlightedId`, which will work even if the `letter` object has changed since the last render.

recipe: To support multi-selection, replace a single selected ID in state with an array or Set of selected IDs, and toggle membership by adding or removing the ID from that collection.
trigger_condition: You need to support selecting multiple items simultaneously but your current state only tracks a single selection.
evidence: Instead of a single selected ID, you might want to hold an array or a [Set](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set) of selected IDs in state.
